mcqs.question: Two substrings produce the same rolling hash value under Rabin-Karp. What can you conclude?
options: The substrings are probably equal, but a direct character comparison is still needed to be certain
The substrings are guaranteed to be identical, since equal hashes imply equal strings
The substrings must differ, since hash collisions never happen with a well-chosen modulus
One substring is a rotation of the other
mcqs.explanation: Equal strings always produce equal hashes, but the reverse only holds probabilistically — different strings can collide to the same hash value under any fixed modulus, however unlikely. That's exactly why Rabin-Karp always verifies a hash match with a direct comparison before trusting it.

mcqs.question: Why does rolling the hash forward by one character cost O(1) instead of O(m)?
options: Because the window size m is always small in practice
Because it only removes the departing character's weighted term and adds the new one, both constant-time arithmetic operations regardless of window size
Because the hash is recomputed from scratch but using a faster algorithm
Because only every other window's hash actually needs to be computed
mcqs.explanation: The roll step is three fixed arithmetic operations — subtract the old leading term, multiply by the base, add the new trailing term — none of which scale with the window length m. Recomputing from scratch would be the O(m) approach the rolling hash specifically avoids.

mcqs.question: Your Rabin-Karp implementation reports a match the moment the pattern hash equals the current window hash, without any further check. What's wrong with this?
options: Hash collisions mean two different substrings can share a hash value, so a match must still be verified with a direct character comparison
Nothing is wrong — equal hashes always mean equal substrings with a well-chosen prime modulus
The hash should be recomputed from scratch at every position instead of rolled forward
This only matters when the pattern is longer than the text
mcqs.explanation: Collisions are a real, if rare, possibility under any fixed modulus, so trusting a hash match without verification will occasionally report a false match. The fix is cheap — one direct comparison, run only when hashes already agree — and doesn't change the average-case complexity.

mcqs.question: What's the benefit of running two independent rolling hashes with different (base, mod) pairs and requiring both to match before verifying?
options: It roughly doubles the speed of the algorithm
It collapses the collision probability to the product of the two individual collision probabilities, making a false match effectively impossible in practice
It removes the need for a direct character-comparison verification step entirely
It allows searching for two different patterns at once
mcqs.explanation: For both independent hashes to collide on the same pair of substrings, each collision would have to happen simultaneously under two unrelated moduli — a probability far lower than either alone, which is the whole point of double-hashing. It doesn't remove the need for a final direct comparison, it doesn't speed anything up, and it isn't about multi-pattern search.

mcqs.question: You need to search a text for 500 different patterns, all the same length. What's the Rabin-Karp approach that avoids 500 separate passes over the text?
options: Concatenate all 500 patterns into one long pattern and search for that
Hash all 500 patterns into a set up front, then make one pass over the text, rolling the window hash forward and checking set membership at each position
Run KMP once per pattern, since Rabin-Karp cannot handle multiple patterns
Sort the patterns and binary search the text for each one
mcqs.explanation: Because all patterns share a length, one rolled hash per text position can be checked against a set of precomputed pattern hashes in O(1), answering all 500 patterns in a single O(n) pass. Concatenating patterns changes the problem being solved, and sorting/binary-searching the text doesn't apply to substring matching.

mcqs.question: In a language where the % operator can return a negative result for a negative operand, what happens if the roll step's modular subtraction isn't guarded?
options: The program crashes with a division error
The window size is automatically adjusted to compensate
The algorithm still works correctly, just slightly slower
The hash silently becomes negative and will never again equal a legitimately-computed positive hash, so matches quietly stop being found
mcqs.explanation: A negative intermediate value under an unguarded modulus stays negative and permanently diverges from the space of valid non-negative hash values, so real matches silently go undetected from that point onward — with no crash and no obvious symptom. The standard fix is adding mod before taking the modulus so the result is forced back into [0, mod).
